questions.question: In a single-item inventory system with backlogging, what is the inventory level $I_k$ at the start of period $k$?
options: On-hand stock plus outstanding orders minus backlogged demand.
On-hand stock minus backlogged demand, which may be negative.
On-hand stock only, so the level can never be negative.
Cumulative demand minus cumulative deliveries so far.

questions.question: In a single-item inventory system with backlogging and lead time $l\ge1$, which events change the inventory level $I_k$?
options: Placing an order raises it at once by the order size, and demand lowers it.
Demand lowers it only while stock is on hand; excess demand leaves it unchanged.
Only deliveries and orders change it; backlogged demand is recorded separately.
Demand lowers it at once and a delivery raises it on arrival; placing an order does not.

questions.question: In a single-item inventory system with backlogging, the inventory level $I_k$ has parts $I_k^+=\max\{I_k,0\}$ and $I_k^-=\max\{-I_k,0\}$. Which statement holds for every possible value of $I_k$, positive or negative?
options: $I_k^+I_k^-=0$: on-hand stock and backlog are never both positive.
$I_k^++I_k^-=I_k$: the level is the sum of stock and backlog.
$I_k^-=-I_k^+$: the backlog is the negative of the on-hand stock.
$I_k^+\ge I_k^-$: the on-hand stock never falls below the backlog.

questions.question: For a single-item inventory system written with $I_k$, $I'_k$, $I_k^+$ and $I_k^-$, what does $I_k^+$ denote?
options: The inventory level at the end of period $k$, after demand $D_k$.
The level at the start of period $k$ plus all outstanding orders.
The inventory on hand at the start of period $k$, $\max\{I_k,0\}$.
The backlogged demand at the start of period $k$, $\max\{-I_k,0\}$.

questions.question: With lead time $l\ge1$, the inventory level follows $I_k=I'_{k-1}+Q_{k-l}$, where $Q_j$ is the order placed at the start of period $j$. At the start of which period does $Q_j$ raise the level?
options: Period $j$, the period in which it is placed.
Period $j+l$, exactly $l$ periods after placement.
Period $j+l-1$, one period before the lead time ends.
Period $j+l+1$, the period after the lead time ends.

questions.question: A single-item inventory system with backlogging has inventory level $I_k=-3$ at the start of period $k$. What are the on-hand stock $I_k^+$ and the backlog $I_k^-$?
In a single-item system with backlogging, period $k-1$ starts with level $I_{k-1}=5$ and has demand $D_{k-1}=7$; an order $Q_{k-l}=4$ arrives at the start of period $k$. What is $I_k$?

In a single-item system with backlogging, period $k$ starts with inventory level $I_k=2$ and has demand $D_k=5$. Holding cost $h=1$ and backlog cost $b=4$ per unit per period are charged once per period as $hI_k^++bI_k^-$. What cost is charged for period $k$?

In a single-item system with lost sales, demand that cannot be met from stock is lost. A period starts with level $I_k=4$ and has demand $D_k=6$. What are the end-of-period level $I'_k$ and the lost demand?
options: $I'_k=-2$ and $2$ units are backlogged
$I'_k=0$ and $2$ units are lost
$I'_k=0$ and $4$ units are lost
$I'_k=2$ and no units are lost

questions.question: In a single-item system with backlogging, period $k$ starts with level $I_k=3$ and has demand $D_k=5$. How many of the $5$ demanded units can be handed out from stock during period $k$?
options: $5$ units
$2$ units
$0$ units
$3$ units

questions.question: In a single-item system with backlogging and lead time $l$, how is the start-of-period level $I_{k+1}$ related to the end-of-period level $I'_k$? Here $Q_j$ is the order placed at the start of period $j$.
options: $I_{k+1}=I'_k+Q_{k+1-l}$, so the level cannot fall between $I'_k$ and $I_{k+1}$.
$I_{k+1}=I'_k$, since no demand occurs between the end of $k$ and the start of $k+1$.
$I_{k+1}=I'_k+Q_k$, since the order placed in period $k$ arrives one period later.
$I_{k+1}=I'_k-D_{k+1}$, since next period's demand is subtracted at its start.

questions.question: In a single-item system with backlogging, period $k$ starts with level $I_k>0$ and ends with level $I'_k<0$. Which statement about the demand $D_k$ of period $k$ is correct?
options: No demand of period $k$ was backlogged, because the period began with stock.
All of $D_k$ was backlogged, because the level at the end of the period is negative.
$D_k$ exceeded $I_k$, and $-I'_k=D_k-I_k$ units of it are now backlogged.
The backlog $-I'_k$ comes from earlier periods, as new demand is served first.

questions.question: In the EOQ model with planned shortages, backlog occurs because the manager chooses it. In a single-item system with random demand, backlogging and lead time $l\ge1$, when can the inventory level become negative?
options: Only if the policy plans shortages, for example with a negative reorder level, as in EOQ.
Only when no order is outstanding, since outstanding orders cover demand meanwhile.
Never under an $(s,S)$ policy with $s\ge0$, because it keeps the level above $s$.
Whenever demand in a period exceeds the start-of-period level, planned or not.

questions.question: Five periods of a backlogging system have start-of-period levels $I_k=4,1,-1,3,2$ and demands $D_k=2,3,0,3,1$. The ready rate is the fraction of periods that end without backlog. What is it?
Four periods start with inventory levels $3,-2,0,1$. Holding cost $h=1$ and backlog cost $b=3$ per unit per period are charged as $hI_k^++bI_k^-$. What is the average cost per period?

With lead time $l=2$, $Q_j$ is the order placed at the start of period $j$; orders of $Q_{k-2}=4$, $Q_{k-1}=0$ and $Q_k=6$ were placed. The inventory position at the start of period $k$ is $P_k=9$. What is the level $I_k$?

Two single-item backlogging systems start with the same level, no outstanding orders, the same demands and the same orders at the same times; one has lead time $0$, the other $2$. How do their start-of-period levels and positions compare?
options: Levels coincide, but positions differ because the lead-time-2 system counts outstanding orders.
Positions coincide, and the lead-time-2 level is strictly below the other in every period.
Levels and positions both coincide, since lead time delays deliveries but not demand.
Positions coincide, and the lead-time-2 level is never above the lead-time-0 level.

questions.question: With lead time $l=2$, a manager uses an $(s,S)$ rule but checks the inventory level instead of the position: whenever $I_k\le s$ an order of $S-I_k$ is placed. What goes wrong compared with the position-based rule?
options: Nothing changes, because level and position always agree at the moment of ordering.
While an order is in transit the level stays low, so it orders again and stock piles up.
It orders too little, because the level already counts the outstanding orders once more.
Backlog becomes impossible, because the level reacts to demand earlier than the position.

questions.question: An $(s,S)$ policy with $s=3$, $S=10$, lead time $l=2$ starts with $I_1=P_1=5$ and no outstanding orders; demands are $D_1=3$, $D_2=5$, $D_3=1$. If $P'_k\le s$, $Q_{k+1}=S-P'_k$ is ordered at the start of period $k+1$ and arrives at the start of period $k+1+l$. What is $I_3$?

Two single-item systems start period 1 with level $2$, face demands $D_1=3$, $D_2=1$, and receive a delivery of $4$ units at the start of period 2. One backlogs unmet demand, the other loses it. What are their end-of-period-2 levels $I'_2$?
options: Backlog $2$, lost sales $2$
Backlog $3$, lost sales $2$
Backlog $2$, lost sales $3$
Backlog $-2$, lost sales $0$
